turns.boundedConclusion: ZR 37-34 requires the specified transparency on ground-floor-level street walls along primary frontages, subject to the stated exceptions and ZR 37-31 applicability limits. The text gives a 50 percent minimum, a measurement band and several other conditions; it does not by itself establish that the rule applies to any particular property.

materialChecks.criterion: The requirement concerns the ground-floor-level street wall along a primary frontage and calls for transparent materials, which may include show windows, transom windows, or glazed portions of doors.

Transparent materials must occupy at least 50 percent of the surface area of the specified street wall within the band from two feet to 12 feet, or to the ground-floor ceiling height if that is higher, measured from the adjoining sidewalk.

Materials counted toward the 50 percent requirement must not begin higher than two feet six inches above the adjoining sidewalk, except for transom windows and portions of windows separated by mullions or other structural dividers; those materials must have a minimum width of two feet.
The maximum width of a portion of the ground-floor-level street wall without transparency must not exceed 10 feet.

The transparency requirements do not apply to portions occupied by entrances or exits to accessory off-street parking facilities and public parking garages, where permitted; entryways to required loading berths, where permitted; entryways to subway stations, as applicable; or doors accessing emergency egress stairwells and passageways.

ZR 37-31 states that the ground-floor requirements in ZR 37-30 apply in certain areas not otherwise governed by ZR 32-30. It excludes the minimum-transparency requirements of ZR 37-34 for zoning lots in Commercial Districts narrower than 20 feet along the street line, if the lot existed both on March 22, 2016 and on the building-permit application date, and for community facility buildings used exclusively as a school or a house of worship listed under Use Group III(B).

turns.boundedConclusion: BC 1013.1 requires approved exit signs readily visible from any direction of egress travel and sets additional marking requirements where exits or paths are not immediately visible, including marking intervening means-of-egress doors within exits. In an exit access corridor or exit passageway, the maximum distance to the nearest visible exit sign is the lesser of 100 feet and the sign's listed viewing distance.
Exception 1: signs are not required in rooms or areas requiring only one exit or exit access.

Exception 3: signs are not required in dayrooms, sleeping rooms, or dormitories in Group I-3 occupancies.

Exception 4: in Groups A-4 and A-5, signs are not required on the seating side of vomitories or openings into seating areas when signs in the concourse are readily apparent from the vomitories; those vomitories must have emergency egress lighting identifying each vomitory or opening within the seating area.

turns.boundedConclusion: FC 311.1 deems any vacant building, structure, premises, or part thereof temporarily unoccupied and generally requires safeguarding and maintenance under the section. It separately provides that if the property has been deemed unsafe under Article 216 of Title 28, it is to be safeguarded and maintained in accordance with applicable Department of Buildings and/or Department of Housing, Preservation and Development requirements. Temporarily unoccupied premises or parts, expressly including tenant spaces, must be secured and protected under the section. Accessible exterior and interior openings must be locked or otherwise protected against unauthorized entry, including entry by tenants. Fire alarm, sprinkler, and standpipe systems must remain operable at all times except as authorized by the commissioner. Fire-resistance-rated partitions, barriers, and walls, including those separating temporarily unoccupied tenant spaces, must be maintained, with openings, joints, and penetrations protected under Building Code Chapter 7. Owners must remove and prevent accumulations of rubbish and combustible waste by regular cleaning; the stated construction-or-repair exception applies when the work is in accordance with the Building Code and waste is controlled and removed under FC 304. FC 311.4 separately addresses hazardous materials: it specifies facility-closure requirements for unsafe vacant premises containing hazardous materials and for temporarily unoccupied premises containing materials regulated by FC Chapter 50, and thereafter requires the premises to be maintained free of hazardous materials, except as approved by the commissioner. Unoccupied tenant spaces in covered malls have additional requirements: no combustible-material storage; maintained fire separation; at least weekly inspection; secured doors; and no rubbish or other combustible waste.

turns.boundedConclusion: FC 604 requires emergency-power inspection, testing, and other maintenance under an approved schedule established upon completion and approval of installation, and requires written service records. Systems, including appurtenant components, must be periodically inspected and tested under load as directed by the cited NFPA provisions. Transfer switches must be on the maintenance schedule, kept free of dust and dirt, and inspected for contact deterioration; deteriorated contacts must be replaced per the manufacturer's instructions. A transfer-switch test operates it electrically from normal to alternate and back to normal. Recorded standby-power or peak-load-shaving use may substitute for scheduled testing only when appropriate records are maintained. All inspection, testing, and maintenance must be under the personal supervision of a knowledgeable, trained person with at least one of the listed qualifications.

The standby-power or peak-load-shaving exception is conditional: use must be recorded and appropriate records maintained; qualifying use may substitute for scheduled testing, not generally for inspection or other maintenance.
